generatedProse.concept-context: In the School of Sport, a proposal is a framework of questions that turns an interest into a study a supervisor or ethics panel can judge. The questions narrow a broad area, say 'small-sided games and skill development', into a specific, answerable one: which age group, which intervention, which measure, over what period. Across the school the test is the same, though the setting shifts from the lab to the training ground to the community programme. Freshness, not total originality, is the test: a familiar idea tried with a new population, or with a better-controlled design, is fresh enough to be worth doing.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two sport coaching students draft a proposal from the same broad interest in small-sided games and skill development.

Tom writes that the project will study how small-sided games affect young players' skill, because the topic matters to coaches and is widely discussed, and that he will read around it before deciding on a design. The area is named, but nothing is narrowed. It gives no specific question, no age group, no measure and no design. A reader cannot tell what study Tom would actually run, or why this one rather than any other.

Amara drives the same interest through questions. The broad area becomes one specific question: do four-a-side games improve passing decisions in under-12 players more than full-sided games over a season? She says why the comparison matters, summarises what is known and what is not, and sets a workable design against it. The focus is not wholly new, but it is fresh: this comparison, with this measure, has not been run with this age group before.

Both began with the same interest. Only Amara built a framework of questions that turned it into a study.
generatedProse.summary: In the School of Sport, a research proposal is a framework of questions that narrows a broad area into a specific, answerable study and shows its freshness rather than claiming total originality. You can now explain how the questions build the framework, recognise the move from a general area to a specific design, and choose the question that sharpens a topic. The final lesson turns to the report that presents a completed study.

check.body: In the worked example, what did Amara do that turned a broad interest into a study?

items.text: She drove the topic through questions into a specific, fresh comparison with a workable design.
She promised to read around the topic before choosing a design.
She chose a question that was entirely original and had never been studied.
She named the broad area and explained that it mattered to coaches.

feedback.correct: That's right. Amara narrowed the interest through questions into a fresh, workable comparison.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Amara DID to the topic, beyond naming it or promising to read.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara turned the interest into a study by driving it through questions into a specific, fresh comparison with a design. Reading around it, claiming originality or calling it important do not make a study.
